list.listitem: Current guidelines recommend screening for chronic kidney disease (CKD) in patients at higher risk (such as hypertension or diabetes mellitus, age > 60 years, family history of kidney disease, previous AKI, or history of pre-eclampsia) using a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and a serum creatinine to calculate an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). The ideal screening approach, however, is unclear.C
Treat all hypertensive patients with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEI) or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB), unless contraindicated.A

Evaluate men and postmenopausal women for anemia caused by CKD when their serum creatinine level is greater than 2 mg/dL and the hemoglobin level is less than 12 g/dL (<11 g/dL for premenopausal women).C
Treating anemia due to CKD with erythropoietin-stimulating agents may increase mortality, especially at higher hemoglobin targets (level >13.0 g/dL).A

The initiation of hemodialysis based solely on an eGFR between 15 and 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 offers no clinical benefit when compared with initiation in similar patients whose eGFR is less than 15 mL/min/1.73 m2.B
CKD will progress, but the rate of progression is variable with underlying diseases and treatments. B

background.definition: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is the presence of abnormal kidney anatomy or function, for at least 3 months, indentified by either persistent proteinuria or hematuria, by a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2, and/or abnormal anatomy noted on imaging. Diabetic nephropathy is covered in detail in a separate topic. CKD is classified according to cause, glomerular filtration rate (GFR) category 1-5, and albuminuria category (A1-A3). This classification allows for the determination of severity and risk.

list.listitem: In a US cohort study, 9082 patients who participated in the Second National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 1976 to 1980 were followed up for at least 12 years. White patients between the ages of 30 years and 74 years had an incidence of CKD of 7 per 100,000 person-years. For African Americans, the incidence of all-cause CKD was 2.7 times higher. For diabetic and hypertensive CKD, the incidence was 84 per 100,000 person-years.
In the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Study, CKD developed in 4.4 of 1000 white adults and 8.8 of 1000 black adults during a 14-year follow-up period.

In the period of 2003 to 2006, 15% of NHANES survey participants 20 years or older met the criteria for CKD as calculated by the Modification of Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD) equation. This statistic was confirmed by NHANES data estimates from 2023.

A study compared the MDRD study equation with 2 other GFR-estimating equations (Mayo Clinic donors study equation and Cockcroft-Gault formula). It found a more than two-fold difference in prevalence of stages I through IV CKD estimates (11.7%-24.9%), depending on the equation used.

Patients diagnosed with CKD should be staged using the CKD-EPI equation without the race variable. A first-morning urine sample for albumin/creatinne ratio should be obtained to test for albmuniuria.C

Among 2017-2020 NHANES participants with CKD stages 3-5, the prevalance of awareness of CKD was 25.6%. CKD awareness was higher among non-Hispanic black adults (27.7%), men (32.2%), age < 60 years (44.4%), and adults with diabetes (31%) and/or hypertension (26.1%).

The staged prevalence of CKD according to NHANES participant data from 2017-2020 is as follows:
Stage I: 5.7% Stage II: 2.7% Stage IIIa: 3.9% Stage IIIb: 1.1% Stage IV: 0.33% Stage V: 0.14%
In 2021, Medicare expenditures was $86.1 billion, accounting for approximately 22.6% of Medicare spending.
All stages of CKD are associated with increased comorbidity and subsequent healthcare resource use. CKD patients are at least 3 times more likely to be hospitalized than the general population.

A retrospective analysis of 259 patients with CKD demonstrated that 87% had hypertension, 35% had diabetes mellitus, 40% had cardiovascular disease, and 14% had peripheral vascular disease. After a median follow-up of 11.4 months, 47% of these patients were hospitalized, with cardiovascular disease being the most common admitting diagnosis.
In 2019, CKD accounted for 41.5 million disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs).

There are limited data examining the effect of social support on patients with CKD, although several small studies have shown increased rates of compliance and survival associated with higher levels of social support.
Larger randomized trials are needed to assess the impact of social support on outcomes in this patient population.
The burden of loss of disability adjusted life years (DALY) disporportionately impacts those in the lowest sociodemographic groups.

A 2024 review of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' End-Stage Renal Disease Treatment Choices model showed that dialysis facilities caring for higher proporitions of patients with increased social risk (those significantly impacted by social determinants of health) had lower performance scores and experienced notably higher financial penalties.
Important causes of CKD are shown in .
A detailed medication reconciliation should be performed as nephrotoxic medications may contribute to the development of CKD.

The incidence of CKD among patients with relatives with end-stage renal disease was 13.9% using an eGFR of less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2. For our purposes, end-stage renal disease is defined as CKD requiring on-going renal replacement therapy or hemodialysis.

Early CKD progresses via glomerulosclerosis and interstitial fibrosis. Nephron loss causes adaptive hyperfiltration that activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, leading to inflammation, hypertension, proteinuria, and hyperlidemia.
Symptoms are usually not present until the GFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, often found in uremic or stage IV CKD patients, can occur secondary to decreased renal ammonia synthesis or titratable acid (phosphate) excretion.
Subsequent, secondary hyperparathyroidism can develop and lead to calcium deposition in the intima of the vasculature. This may also worsen hypertension.
Anemia may result, as a response to reduced production of erythropoietin, shorter erythrocyte half-life, and abnormal extracellular volume homeostasis.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Note: Table adapted from NHANES 1999-2006, as described in the 2008 USRDS annual report. Participants were at least 20 years of age.

list.listitem: Higher risk patients, such as those with pre-existing hypertension or diabetes, age > 60, family history of kidney disease, previous AKI, or history of pre-eclampsia may benefit from being screened for CKD with a serum creatinine test and urine albumin-to-creatinine assay, but high level evidence of benefit is lacking. B
In patients with incidental detection of elevated urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, hematuria, or low eGFR, repeat these test to confirm presence of CKD. B
Encourage smoking cessation, vaccinations for influenza and pneumococcal pneumonia, and aim for appropriate blood pressure control. B

There are no good prospective data that directly measure the properties, cost, and efficacy of history taking, physical examination, or laboratory screening, and randomized controlled trials that have shown improved outcomes with screening of asymptomatic patients are lacking.

Consider screening for CKD in patients with risk factors for the development of CKD, especially if they have more than one risk factor (see table above). The American College of Physicians does not recommend screening for adults without risk factors for CKD.
As of 2024, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force is reviewing its recommendations for CKD screening.
There is no evidence of benefit in screening asymptomatic individuals without comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes) for CKD.

Screening includes urinalysis with evaluation for protein and a serum creatinine test. For the detection of proteinuria in at-risk individuals, guidelines recommend initial screening with an albumin-specific dipstick. A positive result should be confirmed with a quantitative measurement, such as urine albumin to creatinine ratio.

Evaluate for other causes of anemia, such as iron deficiency, when a patient has a serum creatinine level greater than 2 mg/dL and a low hemoglobin level (defined as <12 g/dL for men and postmenopausal women, and <11 g/dL for premenopausal women).
Measure serum cystatin C when available to confirm eGFR in patients with CKD.
Smoking cessation may help prevent CKD by reducing intraglomerular injury via free radical oxidation and by improving intrarenal hemodynamics.
CKD is considered an immunocompromised state. Patients should be vaccinated for influenza and pneumococcal species.

Hypertension accelerates the progression of CKD. In a meta-analysis of 11 randomized control trials, the risk for CKD progression was lowest for a target systolic blood pressure of 110 to 129 mm Hg. A second and more recent systematic review concluded that for patients with a baseline blood pressure above 140 mm Hg, treatment reduced all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, but that this was not true for patients with a baseline BP below 140 mm Hg.

A long-term follow-up of 840 persons with nondiabetic kidney disease and a glomerular filtration rate of 13 to 55 mL/min/1.73 m2 showed that 60% of patients treated to a blood pressure goal of less than 125/75 mm Hg had developed end-stage renal disease at follow-up compared with 70% of patients treated with a standard blood pressure target of less than 140/90 mm Hg.

Randomized control trials have consistently demonstrated that hypertensive diabetics with CKD have better cardiovascular outcomes when treated for moderate target blood pressures, as high as 150/85 mm Hg. Nondiabetic patients with hypertension and CKD, however, did not demonstrate better cardiovascular outcomes.

In fact, more recent randomized trials of CKD patients have not shown benefit for more intensive blood pressure targets. Specifically, for hypertensive patients with type 2 diabetes, a target systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg conferred no additional benefit. For hypertensive, African American patients, target pressures of less than 130/80 mm Hg conferred no benefit.
Practice guidelines currently recommend a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mmHg.

Titrated therapy with the goal of reducing urinary protein excretion is gaining acceptance as a therapeutic strategy in CKD. The goal for proteinuria is usually considered less than 300 to 500 mg per 24 hours, although the optimum reduction in proteinuria is not defined. The benefit appears to be greatest in those patients with protein levels of less than 500 mg per 24 hours at baseline. However, clinical trials to evaluate this strategy are lacking.

A systematic review of 7 observational studies concluded that patients with moderate CKD could cautiously use occasional, low-dose NSAIDs, with no evidence that this increased progression of CKD. Randomized trials are lacking, though.
In critically ill patients with severe metabolic acidosis, sodium bicarbonate infusion reduced the need for renal replacement therapy.

Empagliflozin: An RCT of patients with T2DM, cardiovascular disease, and a GFR of at least 30 ml/min/1.73m2 found that use of the medication slowed progression to the need for renal replacement slightly (0.3% vs 0.6%, NNT = 333 over 3.3 years) and doubling of serum creatinine (1.5% vs 2.6%, NNT = 90 over 3.3 years).

Canagliuflozin: An RCT randomized 4401 persons with T2DM and GFR 30 to 89 ml/min/1.73/m2 to canagliflozin 100 mg orally once daily or matching placebo. The risk of end-stage renal disease (GFR <15) or initiation of dialysis was slightly lower in the canagliflozin group (NNT = 111/year).

Folic acid: A large Chinese RCT (where the food supply is not routinely supplemented with folic acid) found that enalapril 10 mg + 0.8 mg folic acid daily slowed progression of chronic kidney disease compared with enalapril alone.
Dietary sodium restriction of less than 2,000mg to 2,300mg and a moderate-intensity exercise regimen of at least 150 minutes per week may limit progression of CKD.
Dietary protein should be limited to 0.6 to 0.8g/kg/day in patients with CKD stage 3 or 4, as this may reduce CKD progression.
Abnormal laboratory studies or anatomy on imaging must persist for more than 3 months. C
Stages III to V CKD can be diagnosed by a persistent eGFR of less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2.C

The ratio of urine albumin to creatinine is relatively constant throughout the day, correlates well with 24-hour protein excretion, and is now the test of choice for quantifying urine proteinuria in most circumstances. A first-morning urine sample improves accuracy. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Hydronephrosis on ultrasound, benign prostatic hyperplasia
Renal artery stenosis, inappropriate increase in creatinine with an ACEI
History and exam, will improve with treatment

list.listitem: See for the stages of CKD.

Individuals without kidney damage and a GFR of 60 to 89 mL/min/1.73 m2 can be classified as having decreased GFR. Decreased GFR without kidney injury is common in the elderly. The significance of age-related decline in GFR has not been extensively studied.

The normal rate of albumin excretion is less than 20 mg per day. Microalbuminuria ranges from 30 to 300 mg per day and is persistent. However, it is not specific to kidney disease and can be secondary to systemic inflammation from infections, smoking, or obesity.

The KDOQI guidelines endorse the use of office dipstick, including albumin-specific dipstick testing for screening purposes, but recommend that positive results be confirmed by a quantitative test such as a urine albumin/creatinine ratio. However, dipstick testing may lack sufficient reliability, sensitivity, and specificity to detect proteinuria in at-risk groups.
Spot urine protein levels are affected by hydration status and may vary throughout the day. Timed or 24-hour urine collections are cumbersome.

Albuminuria is defined as the persistent excretion of 300 to 1000 mg of albumin per day, while proteinuria is the presence of between 1 and 3.5 g of protein per day. Nephrotic range proteinuria is greater than 3g per 24 hours.

Evaluate for other causes of anemia, such as iron deficiency, when a patient has a serum creatinine level greater than 2 mg/dL and a hemoglobin level of less than 12 g/dL for men and postmenopausal women (<11 g/dL for premenopausal women).
Iron deficiency in CKD patients is characterized by a serum ferritin level of less than 100 ng/mL and a transferrin saturation of less than 20%.

NICE guidelines recommend an ultrasound in patients with CKD who have accelerated progression, hematuria, obstructive symptoms, family history of polycystic kidney disease, GFR less than 30, or are otherwise felt to require a renal biopsy.

The frequency of monitoring GFR increases with increasing severity of disease. NICE guidelines recommend monitoring once annually for patients with GFR 45 to normal range, twice annually for 15 to 44, and 4 times annually if GFR is less than 15.
Exome sequencing identified genetic disorders in 9.3% of a series of 3037 patients with CKD.
Kidney biopsy should be considered if the information obtained would support identification of cause, enhance understanding of prognosis, and guide treatment.

The Cockcroft-Gault formula was based on measured creatinine clearances ranging from 30 to 130 mL/min/1.73 m2 in 243 men in 1973. It systematically overestimates GFR because of the tubular secretion of creatinine.

Compared with Cockcroft-Gault and other equations used to estimate GFR, the MDRD equation more closely estimates GFR as measured by chromium 51-labeled EDTA (Cr-EDTA), and is recommended by American guidelines for estimating the glomerular filtration rate.

Accuracy of the MDRD is lower when eGFR is greater than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2, and the formula has not been validated in populations other than Caucasians or African-Americans. There is no formula that accurately estimates GFR in acute renal failure.
Patients diagnosed with CKD should be staged using the CKD-EPI equation without the race variable.

In patients with ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis, a risk score with three parameter (percent normal glomeruli, percent tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis, and estimated GFR at diagnosis) was able to accurately predict the likelihood of ESRD at 36 months with low (0%), moderate (27%) and high (78%) risk groups.

Laboratory studies, including the measurement of serum electrolytes, serum creatinine, eGFR, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, examination of the urinary sediment, and imaging of the kidneys should be performed for all patients with CKD.

All patients with CKD should be evaluated for a specific diagnosis. If the history and physical and laboratory evaluations do not suggest a diagnosis, consider a renal biopsy in a patient who has an idiopathic, marked deterioration in renal function.

Treatment includes the management of underlying risk factor comorbidities, such as hypertension and diabetes; secondary prevention of complications; and disease-modifying therapy, including treatment with an ACEI or an ARB.
Patients should be monitored for disease progression. Some guidelines suggest that eGFR should be followed up every 1 to 3 months, though trials of the optimal monitoring duration are lacking.

Indications for nephrology referral include:
Hematuria Hereditary kidney disease Nephrotic syndrome Rapidly progressive disease or disease progression despite optimal therapy Structural abnormalities High risk of progression to ESRD Severe electrolyte abnormalities Uncontrolled hypertension

Either an ACEI or an ARB should be used as first-line therapy to treat hypertension in CKD, especially if the patient has frank proteinuria. Consider a target SBP < 120 mm Hg based on KDIGO guidelines.A
Treating anemia due to CKD with erythropoietin-stimulating agents may increase mortality, especially at higher hemoglobin targets (>13.0 g/dL).A
The KDOQI recommends nephrology referral for CKD stages IV or V, in addition to other indications as listed above. C
In patients undergoing hemodialysis, monthly high dose IV iron improves outcomes. B
For patients with CKD and type 2 diabetes mellitus, metformin or an SGLT2 inhibitor are first line drug therapy. A
Multiple randomized trials support the recommendation that either an ACEI or an ARB should be used as first-line therapy to treat hypertension in CKD, especially if the patient has frank proteinuria.

A trial randomized 411 patients with stage IV or V advanced chronic kidney disease (median creatinine 3.4 mg/dl) to continue or discontinue the ACEI or ARB they had been taking. After a median follow-up of 3 years, the eGFR was numerically higher in the group that continued to use RAS inhibitors (13.3 vs 12.6 mL/min/1.73 m2), but this difference was not statistically significant. Regarding patient-oriented outcomes, patients in the continuation group had a strong trend toward a lower rate of requiring renal replacement therapy (56% vs 62%; hazard ratio 1.28; 95% CI 0.99 - 1.65).

B oth the JNC-7 and Kidney Diseae Outcomes Quality Initiative (KDOQI) guidelines recommend a blood pressure target of less than 130/80 mm Hg. However, a randomized control trial compared a goal blood pressure of less than 150/85 mm Hg with a target of less than 180/105 mm Hg using either captopril or atenolol. The study found no significant difference between the 2 groups' CKD progression using serum creatinine and urine protein testing after 9 years. A systematic review of intensive BP lowering in proteinuric patients with CKD found some benefit in terms of progression of end state CKD, but did not see a benefit in terms of cardiovascular events or mortality. Additionally, a systematic review found no mortality benefit to blood pressure lowering if the patient's baseline BP was already below 140 mm Hg.

The 2021 KDIGO guidelines recommend that adults with hypertension and CKD be treated to a target systolic BP target of < 120 mm Hg with a renin-angiotensin-system inhibitor such as an ACEI or ARB as first-line drug therapy. Combination therapy is not recommended.
For CKD patients without diabetes or proteinuria (urine protein excretion <500 mg/day), there appears to be no benefit to lowering the blood pressure below usual targets.

In patients with atherosclerosis or diabetes with end-organ damage, ACEIs and ARBs are equally effective in preventing renal complications. However, the combination of an ACEI and ARB increases the rate of patients requiring acute dialysis and of hyperkalemia.

A randomized control trial compared fixed standard doses of benazepril 10 mg and losartan 50 mg with maximally titrated doses of the same drugs, and found a greater reduction in decline of renal function with increasing doses.

Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as diltiazem and verapamil, decrease protein excretion in patients with greater than 300 mg urinary albumin per day. These medications are generally considered second-line or third-line agents. Furthermore, these drugs are contraindicated in patients using beta-blockers, and there is no evidence that they delay progression to end-stage renal disease.

In the FIDELIO-DKD and FIGARO-DKD trials, finerenone (a non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist) was found to lower the risk of disease progression and cardiovascular events in patients with CKD and type 2 diabetes.

A Cochrane review concluded based on a review of 19 studies with 993 patients that recombinant human erythropoietin corrects anemia, improves quality of life and exercise capacity, and reduces the need for transfusions in patients with CKD not requiring dialysis.

However, treating anemia due to CKD with erythropoietin-stimulating agents may increase mortality, especially at higher hemoglobin targets (>13.0 g/dL). Two recent randomized controlled trials found that treatment with darbepoetin to a hemoglobin target of 12.5 g/dL increased the risk of stroke (hazard ratio = 192). At a hemoglobin target of 13.5 g/dL, the CHOIR trial documented a significant increase in cardiovascular morbidity and mortality (number needed to treat to harm = 25 for 16 months).
Thus, KDOQI guidelines recommend initating erythropoietic medications only after shared decision-making and only when the hemoglobin is <10 gm/dL, with a treatment target no higher than 11.5 gm/dL.

Roxadustat stimulates erythropoiesis and regulates iron metabolism, and has been studied in patients with chronic kidney disease including patients on dialysis. It was found to increase hemoglobin by approximately 2 gm/dl but increased the risk of hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis. An FDA panel voted 13-1 against approval in July, 2021. It is approved in China, Japan and Korea.
Valdustat was evaluated for its ability to increase hemoglobin, but was found to increase major adverse cardiac events in participants in a large RCT.
KDOQI guidelines recommend low-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels of less than 100 mg/dL.
A recent meta-analysis, however, demonstrated that statins reduced lipid levels, cardiovascular events, and proteinuria, but not all-cause mortality in patients with CKD.

listitem.strong: Management of diabetes mellitus in patients with CKD

list.listitem: The KDIGO 2022 guidelines for management of T2DM in patients with CKD recommend initial therapy with metformin or an SGLT2 inhibitor. Additional drug therapy as needed for glycemic control includes GLP1 receptor agonists as the preferred 2nd line drug, as well as sulfonylureas, insulin or thiazolidinediones especially if cost is an issue.

The guidelines also recommend a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist such as finerenone for patients with T2DM, an eGFR >=25 ml/min /1.73 m2, normal serum potassium, and albuminuria (>= 30 mg/g or >=3 mg/mmol) despite taking the maximum tolerated dose of an ARB or ACEI.
A 2019 systematic review found that use of GLP-1 receptor agonists provide protective effects against CKD disease progression, all-cause mortality, and cardiovascular disease.
The 2017 KDIGO guidelines recommend that use of phosphorus binders be guided by evaluation of individual values of serum calcium and phosphate.

A systematic review of ferric citrate in patients with hyperphosphatemia and anemia found that it could significantly reduce serum phosphorus levels (-1.8 mg/dl, 95% CI -2.8 to -0.75). It was similarly effective compared with other phosphorus binders at lowering phosphorus, but was also associated with an increase in hemoglobin.

The dosage of warfarin and other anticoagulants must be adjusted in patients with CKD. For dabigatran: 150 mg bid if CrCl >30 mL/min, 75 mg bid if 15 to 30 mL/min. For rivaroxaban (Xarelto): 15 mg po qPM for CrCl 30 to 50, and avoid if <30 mL/min. For apixaban: avoid if on hemodialysis. For warfarin: dose is typically 10% to 20% lower.

A systematic review of observational studies found a net benefit to warfarin in patients with non-end stage CKD, but no benefit and an increased risk of major bleeding in those with end-stage CKD.A second systematic review found that the risk of ischemic stroke was reduced 26%, the risk of bleeding increased 21%, and the risk of hemorrhagic stroke doubled with no effect on overall mortality.

An RCT of 2141 patients undergoing maintenance hemodialysis found that a high dose IV iron regimen (400 mg monthly unless serum ferritin was >700 mcg/L or transferrin saturation was ≥40%) was superior to a low dose strategy in terms of the primary composite outcome (29.3% vs 32.3%, p = 0.04, NNT = 33).

Difelikefalin is a peripheral kappa opioid receptor agonist. A RCT randomized 378 hemodialysis patients with moderate to severe pruritus todifelikefalin or placebo. A significant decrease in the Worst Itching Intensity pruritus score (3+ points on a 10 point scale) was greater in the treatment group (52% vs 31%, p <0.001, NNT = 5). Dizziness, diarrhea, and vomiting were relatively common but mild to moderate in severity.

In patients with CKD and a GFR between 25 and 75, with or without T2DM, dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily reduces the likelihood of death (NNT = 48) and the need for dialysis or renal transplant (NNT = 71) when taken for a median of 2.4 years.

In an RCT with 7437 patients, finerenone reduces the likelihood of hospitalization due to heart failure (NNT = 189 per year) in patients with CKD and type 2 diabetes mellitus who are taking maximal doses of their ACEI or ARB.

A meta-analysis found that SGLT2 inhibitors significantly reduce the composite of cardiorenal outcomes in patients with CKD with and without diabetes mellitus (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.57-0.86).This appeared to be a class effect and was similar for dapagliflozin, canagliflozin, and sotagliflozin.

A trial randomized 6609 patients with GFR between 20 and 45 ml/min/1.73m2 to empagliflozin 10 mg daily or placebo. After 2 years, progression of kidney disease or cardiovascular death were significantly lower in the treatment group (13.1% vs 16.9%, NNT = 26).

A phase 2 study randomized patients with stage 3 to 5 CKD and moderate to severe pruritus to oral difelikefalin (0.25, 0.5, or 1.0 mg) or placebo. After 12 weeks, patients taking the 1.0 mg dose had less pruritus and were more likely to have achieved a complete response than those receiving placebo (38.6% vs 14.4%, NNT = 4).
The Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) 2021 guidelines recommend target a sodium intake < 2 gm/day (or < 5 gm NaCl/day).

A randomized double-blind placebo controlled study demonstrated that sodium restriction augments the antiproteinuric effect of angiotensin-receptor antagonists. To maximize the efficacy of ACE or ARB therapy, sodium depletion is recommended through diet or diuretics or both.

A systematic review of 10 randomized trials found that reducing protein intake in patients with CKD reduces death from renal causes by 32% as compared with unrestricted protein intake. The optimal level of protein intake remains unclear.
A Cochrane review also concluded that a very low protein diet probably slows he progress to kidney failure in non-diabetic adults with CKD.
Volume overload is treated with salt and fluid intake restrictions or diuretics.

In an analysis of the ADVOR trial, acetazolamide demonstrated more successful decongestion in patients with acute decompensated heart failure compared with placebo and IV loop diuretics. Ths superior decongestion was noted across the range of renal function, with more pronounced effect in patients with a lower eGFR.

A Cochrane review found 40 studies with 3483 participants comparing hemodiafiltration, hemofiltration, and hemodialysis for ESRD. The overall quality of included studies was low, with a high risk of bias. There was some evidence that hemofiltration and hemodiafiltration may reduce cardiovascular mortality, but the low quality of studies precludes firm conclusions. High flux hemodialysis was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular mortality than low-flux in a systematic review of 33 studies with 3820 participants.

For adults with kidney failure who were judged to be good candidates, a randomized trial with 1360 adults found that high-dose hemofiltration resulted in lower all-cause mortality then conventional hemodialysis (NNT = 22 per year). Note that the benefit was not seen in patients with diabetes mellitus or pre-existing cardiovascular disease.

Only a single trial, reported as an abstract, randomized patients to continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) or hemodialysis, and reported no significant difference in mortality after two years.
A Cochrane review concluded that for patients underoing CAPD, double-bag/twin-bag and Y-set disconnect systems were associated with lower rates of peritonitis.
A Cochrane review also concluded that catheter type (straight or coiled) and insertion technique (laparocopy vs laparotomy) appears to make little difference in the risk of subsequent peritonitis.
In patients on dialysis undergoing coronary stent placement, a meta-analysis concluded that drug eluting stents are superior to bare metal stents.
Studies have generally found that quality of life for older patients on dialysis remains similar to that for other elderly persons.

A randomized trial in patients with septic shock on vasopressors and evidence of severe acute kidney injury compared early with delayed initiation of renal replacement therapy. They found that delaying RRT for at least 48 hours did not increase mortality and allowed some patients to avoid RRT altogether.
A small RCT found that drug coated balloons were much more likely to reocclude than bare balloons following angioplasty for stenosis of AV fistulas.
In randomized trial of 523 patients with CKD, withholding sodium bicarbonate prehydration prior to contrast-enhanced computed tomography did not worsen kidney function.

The KDOQI recommend nephrology referral for patients with CKD stages IV or V. However, this recommendation is not widely followed. In one study of U.S. veterans, less than 30% of the veterans with stage IV CKD were seen by a nephrologist.
A recent randomized controlled trial has suggested that the early initiation of dialysis does not improve outcomes and may increase mortality.
See additional indications for nephrology referral listed above under "Approach to the Patient".
Cardiovascular disease is the most frequent cause of death among CKD patients, and less than 2% of CKD patients eventually require renal replacement therapy.B

Long-term control of blood pressure using renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockade may reduce cardiovascular mortality, but has questionable effect on CKD progression. The effect of long-term blood pressure control using renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockade for nondiabetic CKD has been inconclusive in recent randomized control trials.B
It is generally accepted that healthy patients' eGFR will decrease by 1 mL/min/1.73 m2 per year after the age of 30.

A retrospective analysis of 259 patients with CKD found that 87% had hypertension, 35% had diabetes, 40% had cardiovascular disease, and 14% had peripheral vascular disease. After a median follow-up of 11.4 months, 47% of these patients were hospitalized. Cardiovascular disease (excluding congestive heart failure) or hypertension were the primary diagnoses in approximately 25% of these hospitalizations.
The PREVEND study group demonstrated that increased urine albumin excretion is associated with an increased the rate of CKD progression.

A meta-analysis of high-risk population cohorts demonstrated that hazard ratios for cardiovascular mortality at eGFRs of 60, 45, and 15 mL/min/1.73 m2 were 1.03, 1.38 and 3.11, respectively, compared with an eGFR of 95 mL/min/1.73 m2, after adjustment for albuminuria and cardiovascular risk factors.

Logarithmic albuminuria was linearly associated with log risk for all-cause mortality without thresholds. Adjusted hazard ratios at albumin-to-creatinine ratios of 10, 30, and 300 mg/g were 1.08, 1.38, and 2.16, respectively compared with a ratio of 5. Albuminuria and eGFR were multiplicatively associated with all-cause mortality, without evidence for interaction.
Protein excretion greater than 1 g per day is associated with a more rapid progression of CKD even with high normal systolic blood pressure.
Mortality, cardiovascular risk, and progression of renal disease are all increased in patients with higher levels of proteinuria independent of eGFR.
Among patients on CAPD, elevated NT-proBNP is a prognostic factor for CV mortality, and increased hsCRP is a prognostic factor for all-cause mortality.
Less than 2% of CKD patients require renal replacement therapy. Cardiovascular disease is the most frequent cause of death among CKD patients.

Stage IV CKD was associated with a 17.6% risk of progression to kidney failure and a 45.7% mortality risk during a mean follow-up of 3 years. By contrast, in stage III CKD, the risk for progression to kidney failure was 1.1%, but the mortality risk was 24.3%, compared with 0.07% and 10.2%, respectively, in patients without CKD.

In patients with ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis, a risk score with three parameter (percent normal glomeruli, percent tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis, and estimated GFR at diagnosis) was able to accurately predict the likelihood of ESRD at 36 months with low (0%), moderate (27%) and high (78%) risk groups.
Risk of progression of CKD is highest among patients with significant albuminuria (see
The prevalence and significance of a decreased eGFR in the elderly is controversial.

In one series, an eGFR of less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 had a positive predictive value of 34% for one or more CKD metabolic complications of CKD (ie, anemia, hyperparathyroidism, or serological electrolyte disturbances).

Seniors with CKD have a lower incidence of proteinuria than the general CKD population. Coupled with increased risk for deleterious side-effects, some experts recommend more intensive therapy only if the protein excretion exceeds 1 g per day.
Currently, treatment options are limited, as ACEIs are contraindicated in pregnant women. Patients trying to conceive should be taken off ACEIs and other contraindicated medications.
Pregnancy increases the risk of worsening hypertension, preeclampsia, and preterm labor.

Serum creatinine levels normally decrease through gestation owing to larger circulating plasma volumes. Pregnant patients with elevated serum creatinine levels are at increased risk for renal deterioration (up to the point of dialysis) and even fetal and maternal death.
Patients with history of pre-eclampsia have increased lifetime risk of CKD and should be screened appropriately.

While protein restriction is recommended for adults, data in children with CKD are limited. Two small RCTs found no benefit in terms of disease progression or mortality (total of 250 children studied).
Sixteen RCTs with 809 children with CKD found that one year of 28 IU/m2/wk of recombinant growth hormone resulted in a 3.9 cm height increase compared with placebo. Treatment was well tolerated.
